description:
We are a Brazilian team combining software development, healthcare, and public administration.

At NASA Space Apps 2026, we're building a fire activity calendar using MODIS and VIIRS satellite data and AI-assisted development.

We welcome collaborators skilled in remote sensing, GIS, environmental science, and data visualization.
summary: Firewatch is a web application that compares MODIS and VIIRS thermal anomalies without merging them. For the state of Tocantins, Brazil (2021-2025, the pilot region), it shows for each day the spatial extent and intensity of detections per sensor next to the raw counts, the observation coverage estimated from NASA CMR granule footprints, and the spatial agreement between sensors only where both could observe. It addresses the challenge by making the differences between sensors (pixel size, overpass time, coverage, product version) explicit, so a rise in hot-spot counts is not mistaken for a rise in fire. This matters because counts from different sensors are routinely added or compared as if they were equivalent. Firewatch is experimental and not scientifically validated: a thermal detection is an anomaly flag, not a confirmed fire. Only Tocantins is implemented; expansion to other regions is documented but not yet built. Live app: https://firewatch.ikarusaurora.tech - Open source (MIT): https://github.com/OtalicioAmerico/firewatch-nasa-space-apps-2026
details:
What it does. Firewatch is a historical calendar and map of NASA FIRMS thermal anomalies. For any day from 2021-01-01 to 2025-12-31 in Tocantins (Brazil, the pilot region) it reports, per sensor (MODIS Terra and Aqua; VIIRS NOAA-20), the spatial extent (share of observed 0.25-degree cells with at least one detection, always with numerator and denominator), the intensity (detections per active cell) and the raw detections. It adds the observation coverage per satellite and cell, the spatial agreement between sensors (Jaccard index K with its chance level) only on days when coverage is comparable, the position of each week or month against the available historical reference (always excluding the evaluated year), and an Evidence Explorer that lists the individual FIRMS detections with the SHA-256 and line number of the imported source file. Two coverage scenarios are offered: A (conservative) and B (exploratory). The interface is available in English and Portuguese, in light and dark themes.

How it works. MODIS and VIIRS are not directly equivalent (about 1 km versus 375 m pixels, different overpass times, swath coverage and product versions), so each sensor is reduced independently to a cell-day indicator and their records are never merged into a combined score. Extent is normalised by the area actually covered by the satellites, estimated from NASA CMR granule footprints. Coverage state and detection state are kept separate, so absence of a detection is never read as absence of fire. Weeks are fixed 7-day blocks, and MODIS is compared only inside its own product-version block. Results are exported as JSON with a SHA-256 manifest and served by a static React application.

Benefits and goal. A transparent way to read MODIS and VIIRS hot spots together, showing when a change in counts reflects coverage or sensor characteristics rather than fire activity. In our data, 602,856 detections fall inside Tocantins (MODIS 122,496; NOAA-20 480,360). VIIRS occupies about 2-3 times more cells than MODIS, so raw counts of the two sensors are not comparable. Extent and intensity change the reading of about 18-22 % of the weeks compared with a plain count (for example MODIS block 47/2023: 163 detections, below the available reference, while its extent is above it). A conflict between FIRMS records and the CMR catalogue (Terra, 13-16 May 2025) is detected and flagged.

Tools. Python (standard library) for the engine, validation and exporter; SQLite for research data; TypeScript, React 19, Vite and MapLibre GL for the web application; unittest (147 tests; 28 need the real data) and the Node test runner (47 tests with the derived data); static deployment. Source code and reproduction guide (open source, MIT): https://github.com/OtalicioAmerico/firewatch-nasa-space-apps-2026

Limitations. This is experimental and not scientifically validated: a thermal detection is an anomaly flag, not a confirmed fire, and no independent validation (burned area, imagery) or external expert review exists yet. Five years of history; the MODIS reference per version block has only 1-2 years; CMR coverage is geometric (not cloud-free) and the catalogue has gaps; 0.25-degree cells saturate on very active days; K depends on activity. Tocantins is the pilot: expansion to other regions or global coverage is not implemented; a guide describes what would have to change (docs/EXTENDING_TO_NEW_REGIONS.md in the repository).

Originality and prior work. From 2026-11-09 to 2026-11-13 the author worked in an earlier private project (also named Firewatch): a data foundation, a single-sensor burning-activity calendar and geographic web MVP (published 2026-11-12), first NASA FIRMS samples, a written research specification on harmonizing MODIS and VIIRS, and, on 2026-11-13 (the day the Ceres local event opened), exploratory FIRMS data acquisition and an exploratory MODIS-VIIRS study. Those materials are used only as input and reference. This submission's scientific engine, tools, tests, 2021-2025 Tocantins acquisition and results, web application and documentation were developed from 2026-11-14 (first commit at 09:58). Pre-existing components of the author are reused and declared: generic Aurora design tokens (MIT) and one logo mark (rights reserved by the author); the project name and domain also came from the earlier project. The Git history and docs/PROVENIENCIA.md in the repository document the chronology; no date was adjusted. We understand research and preparation before the official start as permitted and are confirming this with our Local Lead.

Team. Otalicio Americo de Melo Junior (Junior): project owner; problem choice, direction, development and integration. David: critical review of the evidence. Tony: public-utility perspective and fit to the challenge.

Use of Super Intelligence. Claude Code (Anthropic, Claude Sonnet 5.5) was used for AI-assisted software implementation and testing under human direction and review. ChatGPT (OpenAI) was used to structure the development instructions given to Claude Code, support research and planning, review scientific interpretations and analytical results, and draft or revise documentation and presentation materials; we do not claim ChatGPT directly authored source code. Details: AI_DISCLOSURE.md in the repository.
